To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the minimum inhibitory concentrations of antibiotics of vaginal lactic acid bacteria are reported, and the genetic determinants of some of these resistances are described.
the antibiotic susceptibility profiles of vaginal Lactobacilli and Bifidobacteria were determined and that the genetic basis of acquired antibiotic resistances in these strains was identified.

vaginal lactobacilli and bifidobacteria are susceptible to most antibiotics, with the exception of kanamycin, gentamicin and streptomycin, and that acquired resistance is not mediated by genes that can be detected by PCR, with the exception that two Bifidbacterium strains carry an intact tet(W) gene that confers tetracycline resistance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the antibiotic resistance profiles of lactic acid bacteria (LAB) from the human vagina and the genetic basis of acquired resistances.
the identification and characterization of antibiotic resistance determinants in vaginal lactobacilli, and the genetic basis for the acquired resistances.
the antibiotic resistance of vaginal lactic acid bacteria, and the genetic basis of the resistances.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
LAB can act as reservoir of antibiotic resistance determinants but the genetic mechanisms involved in these resistances are strain specific.
LAB can harbor acquired resistances but the genetic determinants of such resistances have not been detected yet in the genomes of LAB.
the vaginal LAB do not represent a reservoir of antibiotic resistance genes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
vaginal LAB can act as reservoir of resistance determinants, but the genetic determinants involved are not always present in the genome of the strains.
the vaginal microbiota is a reservoir of antibiotic resistance genes, but that the genetic basis of the acquired resistances is not yet fully understood.
the vaginal LAB are generally susceptible to antibiotics, but that some acquired resistances can be identified in some of these bacteria.
The main takeaway from our work is that
antibiotic resistance genes can be found in the human vagina, and the genetic basis for some of these resistances can be identified in the genome.
antibiotic resistance genes are not necessarily present in all the strains of the same species and that their detection by PCR may lead to erroneous conclusions.
the vaginal microbiota is not only a reservoir of genes that could be transferred to pathogens, but also a source of genes that could provide protection against pathogens.
